subject: physics_2
question_text: Can there be electric intensity at a point with zero potential? Give one example.

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Two structural checks are IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the two-book union check (the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only) and the past-paper back-test (the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers). Hand-checked: on the equatorial line of a dipole the +q and −q potentials are equal and opposite (equal distances), so V = 0, while the field there is E = p/4πε₀r³ (for r much larger than a), directed opposite to the dipole moment — non-zero. The book's example is correct.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Yes, with the reason
lines: Yes. Potential is a scalar sum, so the +q and
−q contributions can cancel to zero at a
point while their field vectors do not cancel.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say yes AND the reason: scalars can cancel where vectors do not.
steps.why: V adds as plain numbers with signs, E adds as vectors. Two equal and opposite numbers give zero; the two field vectors at the same point need not be opposite, so their sum can survive.
common_mistakes: Thinking zero V forces zero E. The two cancellations are independent.

recall.must_convey: That yes, potentials are scalars and can cancel at a point where the field vectors do not.
accept: V zero does not mean E zero

steps.memory_tip: V is a number, E is an arrow. Numbers can cancel while arrows still add.

steps.label: The example
lines: Example: a point on the equatorial line of an
electric dipole. The two potentials cancel, so
V = 0, but the two fields add to a non-zero E.

lines.text: Equatorial line of a dipole: V = 0, E ≠ 0

steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the equatorial line of a dipole and state both facts: V zero, E not zero.
steps.why: Every equatorial point is at equal distance from +q and −q, so the potentials +q/4πε₀r and −q/4πε₀r cancel exactly; the two field vectors both have a component along the axis, and those components add.
common_mistakes: Writing "axial line" instead of equatorial. On the axial line V is NOT zero.
Saying the fields cancel there. They add along the axis direction.

recall.must_convey: That on the equatorial line of a dipole V is zero but E is not zero.
accept: midpoint between equal and opposite charges
V zero E not zero on the equatorial line

steps.memory_tip: Equatorial: equal distances, so the two potentials cancel; the two field arrows both lean the same way.

insider_note: The examiner reads for the word equatorial — the axial line is the common wrong substitution, and there V is not zero.
